newsitem.title: UK: TENNIS-ANALYSIS OF WIMBLEDON WOMEN'S SINGLES FINAL.
newsitem.headline: TENNIS-ANALYSIS OF WIMBLEDON WOMEN'S SINGLES FINAL.

text.p: Analysis of the Wimbledon women's singles final between Martina Hingis of Switzerland and Jana Novotna of the Czech Republic on Saturday:

Novotna made the perfect start, racing into a 3-0 lead with the match just seven minutes old. Hingis was broken to love in the opening game and managed only one point in her second service game courtesy of a Novotna error. There were already echoes of the 16-year-old's straight sets French Open final defeat to Iva Majoli and Novotna was quick to attack the net to increase the pressure on her opponent. The Czech third seed, showing little sign of the thigh injury which prompted her to pull out of the doubles on Friday, cruised to the first set 6-2 in 22 minutes.

There were more promising signs for Hingis at the start of the second set as she began to strike the ball better and volley with more authority. Two fine backhands past a startled Novotna at the net allowed her to hold serve for 3-2, and when she capitalised on her first break point to squeeze a winner down the line for 4-2 it was her opponent's turn to worry.
Forever haunted by her famous collapse from 4-1 ahead in the final set against Steffi Graf in the 1993 final, Novotna could do nothing about Hingis's first ace which put her 5-2 ahead.
But the world number three showed some mettle in saving four set points at 5-3, even though Hingis eventually prevailed 6-3 in 40 minutes.

Novotna found herself under more pressure in the first game of the final set, hanging on grimly to her serve after saving five break points. It gave her a brief psychological boost and it was Hingis who was reduced to tossing her racket in disgust after missing a cross-court backhand on break point against her in the next game.

At 2-0 up, the title was again within touching distance, but once again it was to prove an illusion. Hingis's extra mobility helped her break back immediately for 2-1 and Novotna, who swallowed a couple of pills at 2-1 and needed an ice-bag on her stomach at 3-2, could not stop the Swiss teenager pulling away to become the youngest Wimbledon champion this century.
